description: The twins, their two mothers and the Narrator — performing the class divide on stage.
content_html:
A Cast Built Around Contrast

Blood Brothers is a play built on pairing. Every major character exists in relationship to their opposite: Mickey, the working-class twin, placed beside Edward, his middle-class brother; Mrs Johnstone’s warm, exhausted love beside Mrs Lyons’s anxious, controlling longing. Understanding how to perform these characters is inseparable from understanding what they represent. When a performer makes gestus choices for Mickey and Edward, they are simultaneously making arguments about class.

Mickey Johnstone

Mickey is the emotional heart of the play. As a child, he is quick, curious, foul-mouthed and funny — a working-class boy who has learned to find pleasure in the limited world of his street. As a teenager, he is awkward and infatuated with Linda. As an adult, he is unemployed, depressed and eventually imprisoned. The arc is from joyful energy to crushed stillness, and a performer must make that arc legible through specific choices at each stage.

Physically, the child Mickey should have a loose, impulsive quality: quick direction changes, a low centre of gravity, hands constantly busy. By the depression scenes of Act Two, that same body should feel heavy and constricted — slow movements, sunken posture, a voice that has lost its colour and pace. On stage, the transition is achieved not through a costume change alone but through physical characterisation. The adult Mickey’s proxemics relative to Linda and Edward in the final confrontation should communicate isolation: if Edward is central and commanding, Mickey is peripheral and cornered.

Key Fact

Mickey’s arc is from working-class vitality to social entrapment. The physical journey — loose, energetic child to slow, heavy adult — communicates Russell’s argument that the class system, not personal weakness, is responsible for Mickey’s destruction.

Edward Lyons

Edward is the same biology as Mickey but a different upbringing entirely. Raised in a large house with books and educational opportunity, he speaks in RP (Received Pronunciation), uses formal vocabulary and carries the easy confidence of someone who has never been told their prospects are limited. As a performer, the key challenge with Edward is to make him genuinely warm and likeable rather than simply a symbol of privilege, or the friendship between the brothers will feel implausible. His physical posture should be upright, open and unhurried — not stiff or snobbish, but belonging to someone with no reason to be guarded.

The contrast between Mickey’s Liverpudlian dialect and Edward’s RP is a central theatrical language. A sound designer should consider whether a soundscape or underscore in the childhood scenes reinforces the warmth of the friendship across that divide, or whether the contrast should feel more pronounced and uncomfortable by Act Two.

Mrs Johnstone

Mrs Johnstone is the play’s moral centre. She is a single mother of seven — later nine — exhausted, behind with the hire purchase, still humming Marilyn Monroe songs because she holds onto the idea that life could be beautiful. Russell asks the audience to love and pity her simultaneously. When she gives up one twin, she does so out of desperation, not cruelty, and the audience must feel that gap between her intent and the consequences.

As a performer, Mrs Johnstone requires extraordinary vocal range. She sings through some of her most painful moments; the songs are not relief from grief but a way of bearing it. In the scenes where she makes the deal with Mrs Lyons, a performer might choose a low, quiet vocal register — someone speaking who doesn’t quite believe her own words. Her proxemics relative to Mrs Lyons in this scene should show social submission: she may be physically smaller on stage, seated while Mrs Lyons stands, positioned towards the edge of the acting space while Mrs Lyons occupies centre.

A costume designer working on Mrs Johnstone might use the visual vocabulary of 1960s Liverpudlian working-class life: worn fabrics, faded floral prints, practical but not fashionable. The fit of the clothes might suggest she has little money for new ones; alterations and visible repairs become design language. This contrasts directly with Mrs Lyons, whose costume should communicate affluence through fabric quality (wool, structured tailoring), clean lines and the absence of visible wear. The two women standing together should read as a class map even before they speak.

Mrs Lyons

Mrs Lyons is a more complicated figure than a simple villain. She cannot have children and she wants one desperately. When she persuades Mrs Johnstone to give up a twin, she is acting from real longing, not purely from selfishness. However, her means are manipulative: she exploits Mrs Johnstone’s superstition about the shoes-on-the-table curse, turning a folk belief into a weapon of social control. As she grows more anxious about the truth being revealed, she becomes increasingly unstable — eventually violent.

A performer playing Mrs Lyons must find the genuine pain underneath the control. Her proxemics should change over the course of the play: early on she is composed, her posture upright and assured; by the later scenes, her movements might become tighter, more restless, with sudden bursts of physicality that signal the loss of control underneath the bourgeois surface. Vocally, she begins measured and persuasive; by Act Two, her pitch rises and her pace becomes erratic.

Key Fact

Mrs Lyons uses Mrs Johnstone’s belief in a local superstition to coerce her silence. This moment is central to the play’s exploration of how the powerful manipulate the powerless — and a director should treat it as a key staging moment, not a throwaway exchange.

A common student error is to describe Mickey as “representing the working class” and Edward as “representing the middle class” and leave it there. This is insufficient for an 8 or 12-mark question. The examiner wants to see how you would perform or design these characters as specific people in specific moments — not as walking symbols. Mickey’s depression in Act Two is not just “what happens to working-class people”; it is a specific person in a specific physical and emotional state. Describe the vocal pitch, the pace, the posture, the proxemics for that named moment. Then, and only then, link it to the theme.
exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark performer question, the single most common error is writing about what a character feels without translating that feeling into specific vocal and physical choices. “I would play Mickey as sad and hopeless in the depression scenes” earns almost nothing. The examiner needs: “I would use a slow, flat vocal pace with reduced volume and little variation in pitch, paired with a sunken posture and minimal eye contact, to communicate Mickey’s emotional withdrawal.” You must name the vocal quality AND the physical choice AND anchor both to the named moment. For the extended staging response, remember to consider how both performer and designer choices can communicate the same meaning — show that you are thinking across disciplines, not just from one angle.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mickey’s arc from energetic child to depressed adult must be communicated through specific physical changes — loose energy becoming heavy stillness — not just through costume or plot summary.
  • Mrs Johnstone and Mrs Lyons are positioned as contrasts: warm but powerless versus controlled but anxious. Their proxemics, costume and vocal registers should read as a class map when they share the stage.
  • Performer and designer answers must go beyond describing characters as symbols — every choice must be named, anchored to a specific moment and linked to its effect on the audience.

practice_questions.text: Name the twin who is raised by Mrs Johnstone in Blood Brothers.
What is meant by the term 'gestus' in performance?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying gestus as a Brechtian performance concept involving physical and vocal choices; 1 mark for explaining that it communicates a character's social or political identity, not just their individual emotion.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a director might use proxemics and levels to communicate the power difference between Mrs Johnstone and Mrs Lyons in the deal scene.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: naming a specific proxemics arrangement (e.g. Mrs Lyons stands, Mrs Johnstone seated; Mrs Lyons centre stage, Mrs Johnstone to the side) (1); naming a levels choice (e.g. Mrs Lyons on a raised step or platform) (1); explaining the effect of this arrangement on the audience's understanding of power (1); linking the staging to the play's class theme (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Russell uses the character of Mrs Lyons to explore the theme of manipulation and power in Blood Brothers. What does Russell want the audience to understand about how the powerful use the powerless?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying Mrs Lyons's use of superstition as a manipulation tool (1); explaining how this reflects a class power dynamic (employer over employee) (1); analysing what Russell intends the audience to understand about systemic manipulation (1); linking to at least one specific named moment in the play (1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Mickey, explain the vocal and physical choices you would make in the moment Mickey confronts Edward during the final scene of Blood Brothers. Refer to at least one vocal choice and at least one physical choice, and explain the effect of each on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names at least one specific vocal choice (e.g. raised volume, broken pitch, accelerating pace) AND one specific physical choice (e.g. advancing proxemics towards Edward, unstable posture, shaking hands gripping the gun) for the named moment. Explains the effect of each choice on the audience with clarity. Demonstrates awareness of the contrast between Mickey's emotional state and the class context. May reference the gestus of the moment.

Secure: One vocal and one physical choice identified with explanation of effect. Choices are generally concrete. Anchor to the named moment is present.

Developing: Relevant but generic (e.g. 'I would be angry'). Some physical or vocal idea mentioned but not named precisely. Effect on audience implied rather than stated.

Emerging: Describes how Mickey feels without translating into performer choices. Minimal or no reference to the specific moment.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would stage the deal scene in which Mrs Johnstone agrees to give one twin to Mrs Lyons. In your answer, refer to performer positioning, a lighting choice, and one further design discipline. Explain how each choice communicates the relationship between the two women to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Treats the deal scene as a power-map between two women from different classes. Specifies performer positioning (e.g. Mrs Lyons standing and moving around a seated, still Mrs Johnstone; Mrs Lyons occupying centre stage throughout). Names a lighting choice with concrete detail (e.g. a warm overhead lighting special on Mrs Lyons drawing focus; a cooler, lower-intensity fill on Mrs Johnstone that visually diminishes her). Introduces a further design element with equal specificity (e.g. costume contrast: Mrs Lyons in structured wool, Mrs Johnstone in worn cotton; or sound: a quietening soundscape so each pause carries weight). Explains the effect of each choice on the audience and links to Russell's social argument. Reaches a directorial decision.

Secure: Covers positioning and two design disciplines with generally concrete choices. Class contrast communicated. Effect on audience addressed.

Developing: Some staging ideas but generic. Positioning mentioned without specifics. Design choices described in general terms (e.g. 'dark lighting for sadness').

Emerging: Basic ideas with no named detail. Little or no explanation of audience effect.

knowledge_checks.q: Which character in Blood Brothers uses a local superstition to coerce Mrs Johnstone into silence?
What vocal register distinguishes Edward from Mickey throughout Blood Brothers?
Mickey's physical journey in Blood Brothers goes from a loose, energetic child to a slow, _____ adult, communicating the social cost of unemployment and entrapment.
In performance, _____ refers to the physical relationship between performers on stage and what the distance between them communicates to the audience.
Match each character to their defining arc or role in Blood Brothers:
right: Working-class twin; arc from joyful child to depressed adult
The play's emotional centre; warm, exhausted single mother
Anxious employer who manipulates superstition to keep her secret

flashcard_questions.q: What is Mickey Johnstone's social background in Blood Brothers?
flashcard_questions.a: Working-class, raised by Mrs Johnstone in a Liverpool council house.

flashcard_questions.q: What is gestus in Brechtian performance?
flashcard_questions.a: A physical and vocal choice that communicates a character's social or political identity.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Mrs Lyons manipulate Mrs Johnstone into giving up a twin?
flashcard_questions.a: She exploits Mrs Johnstone's belief in a superstition about shoes on the table.

flashcard_questions.q: What vocal contrast distinguishes Mickey from Edward in Blood Brothers?
flashcard_questions.a: Mickey uses Liverpudlian dialect; Edward speaks in RP.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Mrs Johnstone's role in the play?
flashcard_questions.a: Single mother of nine; the play's emotional and moral centre.

flashcard_questions.q: What does RP stand for in acting?
flashcard_questions.a: Received Pronunciation — the accent associated with educated, upper-middle-class British English.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to Mickey physically across the arc of Blood Brothers?
flashcard_questions.a: He moves from loose, energetic child to slow, heavy, depressed adult.
The physical distance between performers on stage and what it communicates.
Bringing a character's inner life into specific vocal and physical choices.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Mrs Lyons change physically across Blood Brothers?
flashcard_questions.a: She begins composed and controlled; becomes increasingly restless and unstable.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a soundscape in sound design?
flashcard_questions.a: A layered audio environment that creates mood and atmosphere for a scene.
A character's status, mood and emotional state through how they hold the body.

glossary_terms.definition: A physical and vocal performance choice that communicates a character's social or political identity, as developed by Bertolt Brecht.
The point in the body around which movement is generated; a lower centre of gravity suggests a child's physicality.
The physical interpretation of a character, including movement, posture, gesture and facial expression.
The physical relationship between performers on stage — how close or far apart they stand, and what that distance communicates.
The accent associated with educated upper-middle-class British English, sometimes called 'BBC English'.
The way a performer holds and moves the body, signalling status, mood and character.
A layered audio environment created in sound design to shape the mood and atmosphere of a scene.
A layer of music that sits beneath spoken or sung text, shaping its emotional tone.

items.title: National Theatre Playwrights Series: Style
items.description: How character voice and social identity are encoded in language style — directly relevant to Russell's use of Liverpudlian dialect vs RP to make class division audible.

items.title: Five Truths: Konstantin Stanislavski — National Theatre
items.description: Psychological character creation in Stanislavski's tradition — essential for approaching Mickey's arc from joyful child to depressed adult with genuine emotional truth.

items.title: Movement Direction with Vanessa Ewan: Creating Character — National Theatre
items.description: How physical choices build character — the specific body language, centre of gravity and gesture vocabulary that distinguish Mickey from Edward at every age.

items.title: National Theatre: Adrian Lester on Acting
items.description: An award-winning actor's insights into craft — the kind of specific vocal and physical thinking the exam 8-mark performer question rewards.

items.description: The class system that created the divide between the Johnstones and the Lyons — understanding the deep history of British class enables richer character analysis.

items.title: Five Truths: Bertolt Brecht — National Theatre
items.description: Brechtian gestus in practice — how social class can be communicated through a single physical attitude. Relevant to the contrast between Mickey's and Edward's physical vocabularies.
